SECTION 1
Where he stands
 
The two full practice exams on paper. On Sunday, November 8 (Easiest to Average level) he scored 189 of 212 (89 percent). On Sunday, November 22, a much harder exam where 169 of its 212 questions were Hard or Hardest, he scored 171 of 212 (81 percent).
Nov 8: School Ability 61/72, Reading 48/50, Language 31/40, Mathematics 49/50. Nov 22: 58/72, 43/50, 28/40, 42/50.
Why the second score is lower
The drop is explained by the harder questions. On the 43 questions of November 22 that were at the same level as November 8, he scored 33. That is close to the 37 his November 8 results would predict, and the difference is within normal day-to-day variation.
Thirteen daily 15-minute tests ranged from 19 of 32 to 30 of 32. His lowest, Wednesday, November 25, was also his hardest: 29 of its 32 questions were Hard or Hardest.
Upper panel: percent right on each daily test. Lower panel: share of that test's questions at the Hard or Hardest level. Low scores line up with hard tests.
Every test question since November 8, by level (846 questions). Easiest to Average: 351 of 409 right (86 percent). Hard and Hardest: 350 of 437 right (80 percent).
Language is the only subject below 80 percent at the standard level.
Is he improving? Comparing the first half of the period with the second, at matched difficulty, Reading, Mathematics and School Ability are steady. Language is down about 13 points. The numbers are too small to call this proven, but it is the one subject moving the wrong way.

SECTION 4
Writing
 
Full 30-minute Writing Samples: 3, 3, 3 out of 6 (November 8, 11 and 22). Short daily paragraphs: 3, 4, 4, 4, 2, 4. Writing-skill practice questions: one in 21 days.
On the app's rubric, a 3 means "a clear point, but support is thin, paragraphs wander, sentences repeat and errors are noticeable". A 4 adds specific support and a mostly clear order. The steps from 3 to 4 are concrete:
  • one specific example for each reason;
  • one job for each paragraph, with a linking word between paragraphs;
  • two sentences combined in a different way;
  • two minutes at the end to check capitals, punctuation and spelling.
The app does not export the reviewer's comments, so I cannot quote them here. They are on the Essays card in your parent view.

Exam day
  • His usual wake time; a normal breakfast. Leave so that he checks in at the Trinity Hall reception desk well before 9:00 AM.
  • Before leaving, 10 minutes writing down anything he is worried about. In a study of anxious ninth graders, this lifted exam grades from B-minus to B-plus.
  • On "No mistakes" questions: read every word before choosing.
  • On the Writing Sample: plan for 2 minutes, give one specific example for each reason, and keep the last minutes to check.
  • In the breaks: rest, water and a snack. No last-minute review.
  • What to bring is not published. Please check the school's confirmation letter or email for the items and arrival time.
SECTION 7
How you can help (ten minutes a day is enough)
 
  • Sit with him for the review steps on Friday, Saturday and Monday. Ask, "What rule does this question test?" and wait for his answer before he clicks on.
  • Before a lesson closes, ask him to say the rule out loud. If he cannot, the lesson is not done.
  • Each evening, ask him three rules from his list: capitals in titles of works, "No mistakes", doubled letters, and the trip with a stop.
  • Hold the order: tutoring first, test last.
  • Hold the bedtime. A teenager needs 8 to 10 hours of sleep; tired students score lower.
  • Please do not add worksheets or extra practice tests in the last two days. Rest helps him more than cramming.
SECTION 8
What the app does by itself
 
  • It sends every miss back to him on new questions until he has won it back on two different days.
  • It asks one memory question a day from his most-missed rule.
  • It writes your nightly note in the parent view.
  • Its morning and nightly checks confirm that nothing in it breaks.
